dataSheet.description: A generic light front-wheel-drive hatchback in the 1.2 t class: roughly 100 kW, 2.55 m wheelbase, nose-heavy weight distribution.
sources: Class-typical figures from manufacturer specification sheets for B/C-segment hatchbacks (mass 1150–1300 kg, wheelbase 2.5–2.65 m, Cd 0.30–0.33, 60/40 front weight bias).
Tire feel parameters tuned to a ~0.85 g skidpad and ~38 m 100–0 km/h braking distance, typical of published road tests for the class.
Suspension rates typical of a compact hatchback with ~1.4 Hz front and ~1.5 Hz rear ride frequencies, soft rear bar (Gillespie, Fundamentals of Vehicle Dynamics, ch. 5).
Drivetrain [ILLUSTRATIVE]: a 1.6 l naturally aspirated four (peak 172 N·m, 100 kW at 6000 rpm), five-speed ratios and a 4.1 final drive typical of the class; open front differential.

Steering geometry [ILLUSTRATIVE]: 5–6° caster giving about 25 mm of mechanical trail, a small positive scrub radius and an electric assist removing roughly 60 % of the rack torque at the hand wheel, typical of a modern front-drive hatchback.

Roll centres [ILLUSTRATIVE]: a MacPherson front near 80 mm and a torsion-beam rear near 120 mm above ground (Milliken & Milliken, Race Car Vehicle Dynamics, ch. 17); aero lift coefficients of a modern hatchback are small and positive (Hucho, Aerodynamics of Road Vehicles, ch. 4), with the drag centred a little above the centre of mass.

Travel curves [ILLUSTRATIVE] (ADR-0026): roll-centre height falling with bump and camber gain at rates scaled from the curves derived for Project Chrono's BMW E90 from its hardpoints (MacPherson front: roll centre −2.9 mm per mm of bump, camber about −20°/m; double wishbone: −1.6 mm per mm; docs/validation/chrono-bmw-e90.md), eased for this car's lower roll centres. No toe curves: road cars are set up for near-zero bump steer, and the E90 comparison found toe follows force more than travel.
dataSheet.notes: Not a specific production model. Values are class-representative.
